newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japanese investors still prefer bonds - survey.
newsitem.headline: Japanese investors still prefer bonds - survey.

text.p: Japanese institutional investors plan to continue putting more money into bonds while scaling back their equity investments, a Reuters investment survey for December showed on Friday.
In the survey, compiled this week, few respondents altered their asset allocation preferences from the previous survey, as there are not many potentially market-rocking factors looming.
But those who did not change their weightings suggested they may be approaching a point where they consider a gradual shift of funds from equities to bonds over the medium term.
The average overall portfolio weighting of bonds rose for the fifth consecutive month, to 38.30 percent from 37.83 percent in the previous survey.
The average overall weighting of equities fell to 45.80 percent from 46.67 percent.
The Reuters monthly Global Asset Allocation survey asked 14 Japan-based financial institutions about their recommended investment strategy for December.
Within the equities portfolio, the weighting in U.S. and Canadian shares was raised for the third consecutive month to 38.43 percent, the highest level since the survey started in June 1994.

The respondents said while there may be some short-term risks due to the current pace of the New York market's bull run, U.S. stocks should remain on an uptrend and any correction is likely to provide bargain-hunting opportunities.
Meanwhile, the weighting in Japanese stocks was lowered for the third consecutive month to 29.11 percent, down 0.86 percentage point from the previous survey.
The respondents cited poor earnings prospects of Japanese firms and the incoming supply of new shares as factors that could cap the Nikkei 225 average's rise.
Some, however, suggested the government might consider some market-boosting measures if the benchmark Nikkei average of 225 shares in the Tokyo stock market dipped below 20,000.
Also, some said Japanese stocks were clear laggards compared with other markets, and therefore the risk of further selling by foreign investors was slim.
As for European stocks, weightings in German, British and French stocks were raised, while for other European stocks were sharply lowered.
Within the bond portfolio, the weighting in Japanese bonds fell for the third consecutive month to 15.32 percent, a record low since the survey started.
One respondent said a further liquidity-driven rise in yen bond prices was possible, but room for a further decline in Japanese interest rates was limited.
The weighting for U.S. bonds was raised for the fourth consecutive month to 39.45 percent, the highest level since the start of the survey.
With little possibility of a credit tightening by the U.S. Federal Reserve and with inflationary fears virtually absent in the United States, the outlook for U.S. bonds is positive, respondents said.
Weightings in European bonds were lowered with the exception of Germany, which was raised 0.33 percentage point to 13.18 percent.
In the survey, the weighting of cash holdings was raised 0.40 percentage point to 15.90 percent.
